confirmedGaps.title: Workspace-create POST passes the JWT state_id string straight into the INT workspaces.state_id column
confirmedGaps.location: backend/internal/workspace/handler.go:52-66 (stateID,_ := claims["state_id"].(string); StateID: stateID) -> workspace/repo.go:44-49 INSERT ... ws.StateID into column declared `state_id INT` in migration 005_create_workspaces.up.sql:4
confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: For an onboarded user the state_id claim is a numeric string (e.g. "24") and inserts fine, but if state_id is ever the literal "pending-onboarding" (the Login placeholder, which RequireState does NOT reject because it only checks for empty string — middleware/middleware.go:299-303), the INSERT into the INT column fails with a 500, and the handler returns an opaque "failed to create workspace". The path is type-fragile and inconsistent with the onboarding adapter, which resolves the state code to an int before insert (main.go:464-479).
confirmedGaps.recommendation: Resolve/validate state_id to an integer in the workspace handler/service, and have RequireState reject the "pending-onboarding" sentinel explicitly rather than only empty string.
confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning: I traced the full chain and the claim holds end-to-end. (1) The column is INT: `state_id INT REFERENCES states(id)` in migration 005_create_workspaces.up.sql:4. (2) The handler reads the claim as a string and passes it through untouched: `stateID, _ := claims["state_id"].(string)` then `StateID: stateID` (workspace/handler.go:53,63). (3) The service forwards it with no validation: `StateID: input.StateID` (workspace/workspace.go:118). (4) The repo INSERTs that Go string straight into the INT column: `INSERT INTO workspaces (name, state_id, ...) VALUES ($1,$2,...)` binding `ws.StateID` (workspace/repo.go:45-48). pgx sends a numeric string like "24" as text and PG implicitly coerces it, but a non-numeric string is rejected with 22P02 invalid-input-syntax, which the repo wraps and the handler returns as 500 "failed to create workspace" (handler.go:67-69). The placeholder is real: the login path sets state_id="pending-onboarding" for users with no resolved workspace/state (auth/handler.go:452-453,552-553,728-729; auth/auth.go:571). RequireState only blocks empty string, so "pending-onboarding" passes (middleware/middleware.go:299-303); TenantContext likewise only blocks empty workspace_id (middleware.go:121-124). The POST /workspace route is mounted behind exactly JWTAuth→TenantContext→RequireState (main.go:1269-1278), so a freshly-registered/email-verified but not-yet-onboarded user CAN reach the handler with state_id="pending-onboarding" and trigger the failing INSERT. The inconsistency the claim cites is also real: the onboarding adapter resolves the state code to an int BEFORE insert (main.go:460-487), so the normal product path never hits this — only the direct workspace-create handler is fragile. I confirmed the handler tests use a mock service (workspace/handler_test.go:30-40) that never touches the INT column, so the gap is uncaught by the existing test suite. I held this at MEDIUM rather than HIGH because: no data corruption (PG rejects the row atomically, no partial write), no tenant-isolation/security impact, and the primary onboarding flow inserts a valid numeric string; the failure is an opaque 500 on a reachable-but-secondary path for a pending-onboarding caller. Not a stylistic nit — it is a genuine type contract mismatch between the JWT string claim and the INT column with a real reachable trigger.

confirmedGaps.title: Credit reservation TTL sweeper (ExpireAbandoned) is never wired as a worker — dropped consume/refund permanently double-charges credits
confirmedGaps.location: backend/internal/upload/credit/credit.go:531 (ExpireAbandoned defined) vs grep shows zero production callers; backend/cmd/api/main.go:1680-1693 wires the gate but registers no expire worker; relied-upon comments at backend/internal/handler/chunked_upload.go:428, 765, 840
confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: Every code path that drops a Consume/Refund — cold-path finalize where credit_reservation_id is NULL (chunked_upload.go:620-626 passes nil → Consume no-ops), a failed Refund on cancel/finalize (logged only, chunked_upload.go:844-848, 1275), or a LiveGate Consume error after a successful upload (chunked_upload.go:767-772) — leaves an 'active' reserve ledger entry that is never settled. Because the balance rollup counts reserved credits against available, the user is silently and permanently down 1+ credits per stuck reservation with no reconciliation path. The whole design explicitly leans on ExpireAbandoned as the safety net and it does not run.
confirmedGaps.recommendation: Register a background worker that calls uploadCreditSvc.ExpireAbandoned(ctx, ttl) on an interval (e.g. hourly) whenever the credit meter is enabled, mirroring the upload-session-cleanup worker registration.
confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning: Confirmed the gap by reading the code. (1) ExpireAbandoned (credit.go:534) has zero production callers — grep across backend/ shows it only in its own definition, two test files (credit_test.go:175, credit_integration_test.go:220), and three reliance comments in chunked_upload.go (428, 765, 840). No worker/scheduler/pg_cron invokes it. (2) The two upload-credit workers that ARE wired do NOT call it: upload_session_cleanup_worker.go (sweep, lines 93-139) only aborts R2 multipart state + deletes upload_sessions rows, never touching upload_ledger_entries; upload_monthly_grant_worker.go (line 123) only calls GrantMonthly. The m6Scheduler registers only monthly-payout-calculation (main.go:2061). The streaming ReconciliationWorker is a separate subsystem. (3) The drop paths are real: cold-path finalize passes nil reservation when credit_reservation_id is NULL → gate.Consume/Refund no-op (chunked_upload.go:620-626; gate.go:156-158); success-path Consume failure is log-only (chunked_upload.go:767-772); cancel/finalize Refund failures are log-only (chunked_upload.go:844-848, logRefundFailure 1275). (4) The over-charge mechanism is verified against migration 101: trigger sets total_credits = total_credits + NEW.amount_credits; a reserve posts negative amount (credit.go:287) decrementing total_credits/available, and only consume/refund/expire offset it. With none firing, available stays permanently down — no reconciliation path. The design comment at credit.go:14 explicitly states the TTL expiry 'is run by a background worker' that does not exist. I lowered severity HIGH→MEDIUM because the whole meter path is opt-in and OFF by default: LiveGate (which posts ledger entries) is wired only when UPLOAD_CREDIT_METER_ENABLED=true (main.go:1682-1687); otherwise NoopGate posts nothing. The data-loss-of-credits effect only materializes once an operator enables the meter, at which point it is a genuine silent unbounded over-charge with no automated remediation.

confirmedGaps.title: Asset can land permanently with no WebP derivatives (broken gallery thumbnails) when cwebp is unavailable or the thumbnail worker errors
confirmedGaps.location: backend/internal/handler/chunked_upload.go:957 sets Status='processing' and never publishes a derivative job; sole driver is the poll worker backend/internal/worker/thumbnail_worker.go:176-194 which on GenerateAll error sets status='error' (line 187); GenerateAll fails the whole batch if any variant fails incl. missing cwebp (backend/internal/service/thumbnail_service.go:211-213, 358-359). ProcessingPipeline NATS path is unused (no NewProcessingPipeline call in main.go).
confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: WebP derivatives are mandated for every upload (hardcode law), but generation is best-effort and out-of-band. If cwebp is missing on the worker host, the storage Get fails, the image is an unsupported format (HEIC), or any single variant errors, the asset is flipped to status='error' (or stuck 'processing' if the worker never runs) with empty thumbnail_urls. The gallery then renders broken thumbnails for an asset the user was already charged a credit and quota for, with no automatic retry once status leaves 'processing'.
confirmedGaps.recommendation: Treat derivative generation as a guaranteed step: either generate synchronously in finalize, or add a durable retry/dead-letter for status='error' assets and surface the failure to the uploader instead of leaving silently-broken assets.
confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning: The claim's mechanics are accurate but its severity-driving conclusion ("lands permanently / broken thumbnails / no automatic retry") is refuted by code the auditor missed. (1) RETRY EXISTS AND IS WIRED: AssetRepo.RetryFailedByGallery (asset_repo.go:392-410) resets status='error' rows back to 'processing' and clears processing_error; it is exposed via a live, workspace-scoped route POST /api/v1/galleries/{galleryId}/assets/retry-failed (routes_m2.go:118 -> processing_status_handler.go:86 BulkRetry). The always-running poll worker then re-picks them up. So "no automatic retry once status leaves 'processing'" is false. confirmedGaps.location: backend/internal/worker/upload_session_cleanup_worker.go:119-137 aborts multipart + deletes row but makes no ReleaseUploadReservation call (no StorageAccounting dependency on the worker at all); reservation is only released on the explicit DELETE/Cancel path (chunked_upload.go:831-835)

ListExpired (upload_sessions_repo.go:241) selects expired non-completed sessions and the worker deletes the row, after which the reservation can never be reclaimed, so the leak is permanent (not self-healing). confirmedGaps.title: user_auth_methods has no UNIQUE constraint and is never read — provider_subject binding is decorative
confirmedGaps.location: backend/internal/database/migrations/003_create_auth.up.sql:18-23 and backend/cmd/api/oauth_store.go:84-95
confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: (a) The strong identity key (Google sub) is recorded but ignored, so identity is effectively keyed on the mutable email address — reinforcing S1-G1. (b) Because there is no uniqueness on (provider, provider_subject), the same Google identity can be linked to multiple distinct user rows (e.g., if an email is reassigned or via the S1-G1 path), with no DB guard. (c) If a Google account's email later changes/reassigns, the system has no way to recognize it is the same subject, nor to prevent a second user binding to the same subject.
confirmedGaps.recommendation: Add `UNIQUE (provider, provider_subject)` (and consider `UNIQUE (user_id, provider)`) in a new migration, then make HandleGoogleCallback prefer lookup by (provider, provider_subject) before falling back to email, binding identity to the immutable subject rather than the email.
confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning:
I attempted to refute this and could not. Every factual sub-claim checks out against the actual code, and I found no compensating control elsewhere.

SCHEMA: backend/internal/database/migrations/003_create_auth.up.sql:18-23 defines user_auth_methods with only a PK on id and FK on user_id — no UNIQUE on (provider, provider_subject) nor (user_id, provider). I grepped the entire migrations dir and Go tree: the table is referenced ONLY by 003 (create), 003.down (drop), and oauth_store.go LinkOAuth. No later migration, ALTER, or CREATE INDEX adds any uniqueness (grep returned exit 1 = no other refs).

WRITE-ONLY: LinkOAuth (oauth_store.go:84-95) INSERTs with WHERE NOT EXISTS keyed on the full (user_id, provider, provider_subject) triple. That only suppresses an exact-duplicate row for the SAME user; it does nothing to stop the same (provider, provider_subject) from binding to a DIFFERENT user_id. A grep for user_auth_methods shows zero SELECTs anywhere — the table is purely written, never read.

LOGIN DECISION: HandleGoogleCallback (auth.go:702-766) resolves identity exclusively via existing := FindByEmail(profile.Email) at auth.go:722. The Google sub (profile.ProviderID, populated from payload.Sub in google_provider.go:111) is passed to LinkOAuth at lines 728 and 765 but is never compared on subsequent logins. The UserStore interface (auth.go:69-78) has no lookup-by-subject method at all — there is no code path that could read the stored subject.

CONSEQUENCES: (a) CONFIRMED — identity is effectively keyed on the mutable email, not the immutable Google sub. (b) CONFIRMED at schema level — nothing (DB or app) prevents one Google sub from mapping to multiple user rows. (c) CONFIRMED as a consequence — an email change/reassignment makes the same sub appear as a new identity, and there is no guard against a second user binding the same subject.

NUANCE ON SEVERITY: One mitigating fact the claim omits — users.email is itself UNIQUE (002_create_users.up.sql:3). So you cannot trivially get two ACTIVE users sharing the same current email; the multi-bind-to-one-subject scenario requires an email to actually be freed and reassigned (e.g., Google account email change, corporate mailbox reassignment, deleted-then-recreated account). This is the classic 'email is not a stable identifier' OAuth weakness — it is real and matters for account-takeover-via-email-reassignment, but it is a latent identity-model weakness rather than an actively-broken core flow with a trivial day-1 exploit. The strong-key-recorded-but-ignored design is genuinely decorative as the auditor states. I am adjusting CLAIMED HIGH down to MEDIUM: the binding is real and the subject is genuinely never consulted (so HIGH's 'data-integrity / silent breakage' framing is partly apt), but the email-UNIQUE constraint and the requirement of an email-reassignment precondition keep it out of the always-exploitable CRITICAL/HIGH tier.

Split verdict — the claim bundles two distinct things.

confirmedGaps.title: Signed OAuth state is replayable within its 10-minute window — no single-use consume and no browser binding (CSRF nonce is decorative)
confirmedGaps.location: backend/internal/auth/auth.go:807-839 (consumeSignedState validates HMAC + ExpiresAt but never checks or consumes Nonce); auth.go:649-653 (Nonce field present but unused on verify); no SetCookie for oauth state anywhere — backend/internal/auth/handler.go:914,926 are the only SetCookie calls, both for refresh_token
confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: The primary state path (active whenever GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET is set, i.e. production) is a stateless HMAC token with no per-browser binding and no replay protection: the same captured state value can be presented multiple times until expiry, and there is no cookie tying the state to the initiating browser. This weakens the OAuth CSRF/login-fixation defense the state parameter is supposed to provide. The in-memory fallback path (auth.go:798-804) IS single-use (map delete) but only runs when no signing key is configured.
confirmedGaps.recommendation: Set an HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax oauth_state cookie carrying the nonce in InitiateGoogleAuth and require it to equal the callback state's nonce in consumeSignedState; additionally track consumed nonces (Valkey/short TTL) to make signed state single-use.
confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning:
I read the full OAuth flow and the claim's technical assertions all hold. (1) The signed-state path is the production path: signState (auth.go:776-791) returns a token whenever stateSigningKey() is non-empty, and stateSigningKey() returns ClientSecret when set (auth.go:769-773). InitiateGoogleAuth prefers the signed token (auth.go:677-682). So whenever GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET is configured, the HMAC token is used. (2) consumeSignedState (auth.go:807-839) validates only the HMAC and ExpiresAt (line 835) and returns payload.ReturnTo. It never reads payload.Nonce and never records the token as consumed — there is no map delete, no DB/Valkey write. I grepped the entire backend/internal tree for nonce/replay/consumed/used_state tracking tied to OAuth and found none (the only replay hits are Cloudflare webhook signature and stream replay URLs, unrelated). The Nonce field is written at auth.go:678 and never read anywhere. (3) No state cookie exists: the only two http.SetCookie calls in the auth package (handler.go:914, 926) are both the refresh_token cookie; OAuthGoogle (handler.go:655-673) issues a 302 redirect with zero Set-Cookie, and OAuthGoogleCallback (handler.go:697-716) reads state purely from the query string with no cookie comparison. So there is genuinely no per-browser binding and no single-use consumption on the signed path — a captured state value is replayable for the full 10-minute window. The claim is factually accurate.

However, two things temper the severity. First, the stateless design is intentional and documented: TestGoogleOAuth_StateSurvivesBackendInstanceSwitch (oauth_service_test.go:130-155) deliberately initiates on one OAuthService instance and completes the callback on a *different* instance, asserting success — i.e. the signed token is purpose-built to survive multi-node deploys without a shared store. A naive single-use map (the fallback at auth.go:798-804) only works on a single node and is the path they moved away from. Second, the practical exploit value is limited: the state still carries an HMAC-signed, 10-minute-expiry, per-request-random Nonce that an attacker cannot forge, and the only data it controls is returnTo, which is independently constrained — OAuthGoogleCallback passes returnTo through buildFrontendLoginRedirect and InitiateGoogleAuth derives returnTo from sanitizeFrontendOrigin (handler.go:661-664), bounding open-redirect abuse. The realistic residual risk is a login-CSRF / fixation weakening (the classic reason for browser-bound state), not token theft or tenant-isolation breakage, and it requires an attacker to first capture a victim's freshly-minted state within 10 minutes. That is a real but narrow hardening gap, not a broken core flow or an isolation hole, so I down-adjust from the claimed MEDIUM to LOW.

confirmedGaps.title: Canonical onboarding bootstrap ignores errors from the workspace_members and workspace_storage inserts
confirmedGaps.location: backend/cmd/api/main.go:514-519 (`_, _ = o.pool.Exec(... INSERT INTO workspace_members ...)`) and 524-529 (`_, _ = o.pool.Exec(... INSERT INTO workspace_storage ...)`)
confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: CreateWorkspace returns success (and onboarding advances to step=complete) even if the membership or quota insert silently fails. A workspace can therefore exist with no workspace_storage row (dashboard widget degrades to plan-default via GetUsage fallback, storage_accounting_service.go:140-142) and/or no workspace_members row (AuthLookup falls back to the owner query, auth_lookup.go:51-62). Because onboarding then reaches step=complete, the idempotent short-circuit (onboarding.go:211-213) prevents a retry from ever re-attempting these inserts, so the gap is permanent for that workspace.
confirmedGaps.recommendation: Wrap workspace + members + quota inserts in a single transaction (or check RowsAffected and return an error so onboarding does NOT advance to complete), making the four-way co-creation atomic.
confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning:
The mechanical facts in the claim are accurate, but its central impact thesis is refuted by purpose-built fallbacks that turn both missing rows into graceful degradation rather than breakage.

CONFIRMED facts: (1) Both inserts discard errors via `_, _ = o.pool.Exec(...)` at main.go:515-519 and 524-529, and CreateWorkspace returns `ws.ID, nil` unconditionally at main.go:531. (2) wsSvc.Create does NOT create the membership row itself — workspace.go:104-142 only calls repo.Create (which inserts into `workspaces` only, repo.go:44-49), provisions a bucket, and publishes an event — so the main.go:515-519 Exec is the sole creator of the owner membership during onboarding. (3) Ordering is CreateWorkspace (onboarding.go:273-281) → Upsert StepComplete (289-297), and the short-circuit at onboarding.go:211-213 prevents the onboarding path from re-attempting on retry. So a silently-failed secondary insert is not re-attempted by onboarding.

REFUTED impact: The claim's two cited fallbacks are not accidental degradations — they are designed handlers that fully cover the onboarding case. (a) Missing workspace_storage: GetUsage uses a LEFT JOIN and substitutes the plan-default quota (storage_accounting_service.go:124-142), AND the row self-heals on the first real upload via the ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE inserts at storage_accounting_service.go:156-166 / 196 / 281 / 439. So the storage gap is neither breaking nor permanent. (b) Missing workspace_members: AuthLookup.GetUserWorkspace has an explicit second query (auth_lookup.go:50-62) that resolves the workspace by owner_id and returns role "Owner" when no membership row exists. The only member inserted during onboarding is the owner, so this fallback covers 100% of the onboarding case — the owner is never locked out.

Net: real code smell (swallowed Exec errors lose log/alert signal and the inserts are non-transactional with the workspace create), but no broken contract, no tenant-isolation hole, no permanent breakage. Every downstream consumer already tolerates the missing row. Downgrade MEDIUM -> LOW.

confirmedGaps.title: Successful finalize whose MarkCompleted write fails is later misclassified as abandoned and reaped
confirmedGaps.location: finalize treats MarkCompleted as best-effort and only logs on failure (backend/internal/handler/chunked_upload.go:988-994); ListExpired selects WHERE completed_at IS NULL AND expires_at < now() (backend/internal/repository/upload_sessions_repo.go:251); the sweeper then aborts the (already-completed) multipart and deletes the row (upload_session_cleanup_worker.go:119-137)
confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: If completed_at fails to persist after a successful asset insert, the session keeps completed_at=NULL. After TTL the cleanup worker treats it as abandoned, issues AbortMultipartUpload against an already-completed object (benign), and deletes the session row. The asset itself survives, but the storage reservation for it is double-handled (committed at finalize, and the sweeper would also try to release it once gap #5 is fixed), and the credit ExpireAbandoned (if ever wired) could refund a reservation whose upload actually succeeded — i.e. a free upload. This is the exact silent-misclassification the code comment at 991 warns about, but there is no compensating guard.

confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning: The factual premise holds but every claimed harm is benign or unwired. PREMISE (true): MarkCompleted is best-effort and only logs on failure (chunked_upload.go:988-994); ListExpired filters WHERE completed_at IS NULL AND expires_at < now() (upload_sessions_repo.go:251); the sweeper aborts the multipart then deletes the row (worker/upload_session_cleanup_worker.go:119-137). So a finalize whose completed_at stamp fails to persist WILL be picked up by the sweeper. HARM 1 (multipart abort) — true but benign and self-correcting: after CompleteMultipartUpload the abort returns a benign error, and the worker logs+`continue`s WITHOUT deleting the row (worker.go:122-129). HARM 2 (row deleted, asset orphaned) — REFUTED: the asset row is independent and already committed via persistAssetOrCleanup (969) + CommitUploadReservation into durable used_bytes (978-986); deleting the GC session row is the intended terminal state, and in this case the abort error actually prevents the delete entirely. HARM 3 (storage reservation double-handled / sweeper releases it 'once gap #5 fixed') — speculative and conditional on a hypothetical future change; the current sweeper never touches storage accounting, it only aborts multipart and deletes the DB row. HARM 4 (ExpireAbandoned refunds a successful upload = free upload) — REFUTED on two grounds: (a) ExpireAbandoned is NOT wired anywhere in cmd/api/main.go (grep shows only tests + the unused method; the cleanup worker registered at main.go:1829 is the storage sweeper, not a credit worker), and (b) even if wired, ExpireAbandoned keys off upload_ledger_entries consume/refund/expire child rows (credit.go:541-552), not off completed_at; the success path calls Consume (chunked_upload.go:767) in the CALLER after finalizeUpload returns — and that Consume runs regardless of the MarkCompleted failure because the failure is swallowed at 993 and success is still returned (722/762/774). A consume entry protects the reservation from refund. So there is no billing/data harm. The only real residual is cosmetic/operational: a committed-asset session with completed_at=NULL will be retried by the sweeper on every poll (abort benign-errors -> continue -> never deleted), producing repeating log lines and a stuck DB row — gated on a rare DB write failure in the narrow window between the asset commit and the completed_at stamp. This is LOW, not MEDIUM; no security, tenant-isolation, billing, or data-integrity break.

confirmedGaps.title: OAuth MFA challenge token is delivered via URL query string, exposing a session-issuing credential to logs/history/Referer
confirmedGaps.location: backend/internal/auth/handler.go:766-776 (OAuthGoogleCallback step-up redirect) vs handler.go:487-491 (Login JSON body)
confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: The challenge JWT lands in browser history, the frontend web-server access logs, any intermediary proxy logs, and the Referer header of subresource requests on /login. An attacker with access to any of these (within the 5-minute validity window, before single-use consumption) could complete the step-up. The two login paths are inconsistent in how they handle the same sensitive token.
confirmedGaps.recommendation: Deliver the OAuth challenge token out-of-band like the password path: set it in a short-lived HttpOnly cookie (mirroring the refresh-token cookie pattern in setRefreshTokenCookie) and redirect with only mfa_required=1, or POST it to a one-time exchange endpoint. At minimum, document the residual-risk tradeoff and shorten the challenge TTL for the OAuth variant.
confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning:
The factual core of the claim is confirmed by direct reading. The password Login path returns mfa_token in a JSON response body (handler.go:488-491), while the OAuth callback places the identical challenge JWT into the redirect URL query string: buildFrontendLoginRedirect(..., {"mfa_required":"1","mfa_token":mfaToken,"challenge":"totp"}) -> 302 Location: /login?mfa_required=1&mfa_token=<JWT>&challenge=totp (handler.go:774-783; builder at handler.go:993-1016 url-encodes params into RawQuery). The two paths are genuinely inconsistent and the OAuth transport is the weaker one. The leak surface is real: the token is in the OAuth callback's 302 Location header, the frontend /login web-server access log, browser history, and the Referer of any subresource the /login page loads before scrubbing. The frontend scrub (LoginForm.tsx:60-77) reads oauthMfaToken from useSearchParams, stashes it in sessionStorage, then router.replace("/login/mfa") — but this is a post-load CLIENT-side replace, so the URL-with-token has already been committed to history and to any server access log by the time it runs. So this is NOT already handled elsewhere; it is a genuine integration gap.

However the claimed impact and MEDIUM severity are overstated. The mfa_token is NOT a session-issuing credential on its own. It is purpose-scoped purpose=mfa_challenge (mfa_handler.go:91, issued at 810) and parseAccessToken rejects it (access_token_purpose_test.go), so it cannot be used as an access token. To mint a full mfa_verified session an attacker who captured the token from logs/history STILL needs a second factor: a current valid TOTP code (verified at mfa_handler.go:434 before any session is issued) or an unconsumed one-time recovery code. The token alone redeems nothing. It is further bounded by a 5-minute expiry (mfaChallengeExpiry, mfa_handler.go:96) and single-use consumption after a successful verify (S-003 denylist, mfa_handler.go:440-449). So the real exposure is one of two factors leaking to logs/history/Referer — a defense-in-depth / confidentiality weakness and a real path inconsistency, not the "complete the step-up with a captured credential" impact the claim asserts. Real gap, lower severity than claimed.

confirmedGaps.whatBreaks: Any future handler moved/added under the /api/v1/dp/* API-key group that reads JWTClaimsFromContext (or GetActorID for audit actor, or RequireWorkspaceRole for authz) will silently 401 or attribute actions to uuid.Nil even though the API key authenticated correctly. The workspace_id IS available (via WorkspaceIDFromContext) but role/platform_role/sub/mfa_verified are not, so role-gated and actor-attributed logic cannot work on this surface.
confirmedGaps.recommendation: Have APIKeyAuth also call WithJWTClaims with a synthesized claims map derived from the verified key (at minimum sub=key owner/id, workspace_id, and a role/platform_role appropriate to the key's scopes), or document that the dataplane group must only mount handlers that read workspace context via WorkspaceIDFromContext/APIKeyFromContext and never via JWTClaimsFromContext. Add a guard test asserting no JWTClaimsFromContext-dependent handler is mounted under the API-key group.
confirmedGaps.refuteReasoning: The mechanical claim is accurate. APIKeyAuth (api_key_auth.go:84-87) sets apiKeyKey, workspaceIDKey, and ctxkeys.WorkspaceID but never calls WithJWTClaims, and JWTClaimsFromContext (middleware.go:40-45) only reads jwtClaimsKey, so it returns nil under API-key auth. Consequently RequireAuth/RequirePlatformRole/RequireWorkspaceRole/RejectImpersonationWrites/GetActorID (middleware.go:491-584) would 401/403/return uuid.Nil if mounted under the API-key group. The two auth paths do expose divergent context contracts. HOWEVER this is latent, not live, and the auditor concedes as much: the only route mounted under the APIKeyAuth dataplane group is the inline /api/v1/dp/ping handler (main.go:2447-2450), which reads nothing from context. A grep for api/v1/dp and APIKeyAuth/RequireAPIKeyScope confirms no other handler runs under this group. The middleware that DOES run there — the Valkey rate limiter helpers APIKeyRateLimitKeyFunc/APIKeyRateLimitMaxFunc (valkey_ratelimit.go:94-117) — correctly read APIKeyFromContext, not JWTClaimsFromContext, so they function. Critically, the security-relevant tenancy axis IS wired: WorkspaceIDFromContext and ctxkeys.WorkspaceID are both populated, and those are exactly what tenant-scoped handlers and the ai package read (download_handler.go:53, asset_handler.go:260, ai/handler.go:875), so RLS/tenant isolation is NOT the broken axis. The missing axis is role/actor (platform_role, role, sub, mfa_verified). The failure mode is fail-closed (401/403) for role gates, not an auth bypass, and the only data-integrity edge (GetActorID returning uuid.Nil for audit attribution) also requires a future handler. Real divergence, but no current break and the most dangerous axis (tenancy) is handled — so MEDIUM overstates it; LOW is appropriate.
confirmedGaps.verifyEvidence: backend/internal/middleware/api_key_auth.go:84-87 (no WithJWTClaims call); backend/internal/middleware/middleware.go:40-45 (JWTClaimsFromContext reads only jwtClaimsKey); middleware.go:491-584 (role/actor helpers gate on JWTClaimsFromContext); backend/cmd/api/main.go:2426-2451 (only /api/v1/dp/ping inline handler mounted under APIKeyAuth group); backend/internal/middleware/valkey_ratelimit.go:94-117 (live dataplane middleware uses APIKeyFromContext, works); ai/handler.go:875 + download_handler.go:53 + asset_handler.go:260 (tenancy axis read via WorkspaceIDFromContext/ctxkeys.WorkspaceID, which APIKeyAuth DOES populate)

refutedGaps.title: OAuth-created users get NULL state_id / no phone, diverging from the registration invariant enforced for password users
refutedGaps.why:
The claim's two load-bearing premises are both false in the actual code, so the alleged "divergence from the registration invariant enforced for password users" does not exist.

1) Password registration does NOT hard-enforce state_id. The Register handler (backend/internal/auth/handler.go:340-403) validates only email, password length/bcrypt-input, and phone (line 363-366). There is NO check that req.StateID is non-nil; StateID is `*int` with `json:"state_id,omitempty"` (handler.go:42). The canonical signup UI confirms this: frontend/src/components/auth/RegisterForm.tsx submits email/full_name/phone (lines 117-121) and never sends state_id, and frontend/src/app/register/page.tsx has no state field. So password users ALSO get users.state_id = NULL at registration — identical to OAuth. OAuth does not diverge here.

2) Onboarding's SelectState does NOT write users.state_id. It upserts the SEPARATE onboarding_statuses table (backend/internal/onboarding/onboarding.go:159-179 -> backend/internal/onboarding/repo.go:105-128 INSERT INTO onboarding_statuses). users.state_id is therefore never populated by the onboarding flow for either password or OAuth users. The repo.go:40-50 comment is aspirational/partial: the column is written only at the INSERT (when a caller supplies it — which the real signup flow does not) or via the generic profile editor (backend/internal/handler/profile_handler.go:82-90), which is equally available to OAuth and password users.

3) The schema and admin tooling are designed for NULL state_id, not broken by it. Migration 002 declares `state_id INT REFERENCES states(id)` with no NOT NULL (002_create_users.up.sql:7). The admin filter index (029:22) is just an index; the admin repo LEFT JOINs states (backend/internal/repository/admin_user_repo.go:250,323,519) so NULL-state users still appear, and the explicit `u.state_id = $N` filter (lines 195-197, 493-495) is applied only when an admin deliberately filters by a state — a NULL-state user correctly not matching a specific-state filter is expected behavior, not mis-bucketing. The repo even documents this (admin_user_repo.go:71-73: "users whose state has not been set during onboarding").

Residual grain of truth (separate, narrower issue, not what was claimed): OAuth Create passes only Email (oauth_store.go:43) so OAuth users skip the phone hard-requirement that password registration enforces (handler.go:363). But users.phone is nullable by design (repo.go:46-47 NULLIF) and phone is best-effort collected at onboarding SetProfile (onboarding.go:235) for both flows. There is no documented users.state_id non-null invariant being violated, and there is no OAuth-vs-password divergence on state_id.
